source_text: Hinc et illa soluitur quaestio, quomodo martyres ipsis beneficiis, quae dantur orantibus, indicant se interesse rebus humanis, si nesciunt mortui, quid agant uiui. non enim solis beneficiorum effectibus, uerum ipsis etiam hominum aspectibus confessorem adparuisse Felicem, cuius inquilinatum pie diligis, cum a barbaris Nola obpugnaretur, audiuimus non incertis rumoribus, sed testibus certis. uerum ista diuinitus exhibentur longe aliter, quam sese habet usitatus ordo singulis creaturarum generibus adtributus. non enim quia in uinum aqua, cum uoluit dominus, repente conuersa est, ideo non debemus, quid aqua ualeat in elementorum ordine proprio, ab istius diuini operis raritate uel potius singularitate discernere; nec quoniam Lazarus resurrexit, ideo mortuus omnis, quando uult, surgit aut eo modo exanimis a uiuente quomodo a uigilante dormiens excitatur. alii sunt humanarum limites rerum, alia diuinarum signa uirtutum; alia sunt, quae naturaliter, alia, quae mirabiliter fiunt, quamuis et naturae deus adsit, ut sit, et miraculis natura non desit. non igitur ideo putandum est uiuorum rebus quoslibet interesse posse defunctos, quoniam quibusdam sanandis uel adiuuandis martyres adsunt, sed ideo potius intellegendum est, quod per diuinam potentiam martyres uiuorum rebus intersunt, quoniam defuncti per naturam propriam uiuorum rebus interesse non possunt.
thought_title: Miracles do not overturn the natural limits of the dead
orientation: Augustine is answering the objection that martyrs must know what the living do, since they appear and grant benefits to those who pray.
pass_a_gloss: From this also that question is solved, how martyrs by the very benefits, which are given to those praying, indicate that they are present in human affairs, if the dead do not know what the living do. For not only by the effects of benefits, but also by the very sight of men, the confessor Felix appeared, whose dwelling you piously love, when Nola was being attacked by barbarians, we have heard not by uncertain rumors, but by sure witnesses. But these things are shown forth divinely far otherwise than the usual order assigned to each kind of creatures has itself. For not because water was suddenly turned into wine, when the Lord willed it, therefore we ought not to discern what water can do in its own order of the elements from the rarity or rather singularity of this divine work; nor because Lazarus rose again, therefore every dead person rises when he wills, or a lifeless person is roused by a living person in the way that a sleeper is roused by one awake. Some things are the limits of human affairs, other things are the signs of divine powers; some things are what happen naturally, other things what happen miraculously, although God is present to nature, that it may be, and nature is not absent from miracles. Therefore it is not for this reason to be thought that any dead persons can be present in the affairs of the living, because martyrs are present for healing or helping certain people, but rather for this reason it is to be understood, that through divine power martyrs are present in the affairs of the living, because the dead through their own nature cannot be present in the affairs of the living.

choices.why: Augustine uses the abstract noun for Felix's sojourn or residence at Nola; 'dwelling' keeps the noun form and the sense of a place where Felix abides as a resident, not a shrine.
The brief identifies Felix as a confessor, not explicitly a martyr; keeping 'confessor' preserves the technical distinction Augustine maintains.
The passive of exhibeo here means divine display or presentation of such appearances; 'shown forth' keeps the divine agency implicit and the public, manifest character.
Uirtutes here are divine powers or mighty works, not human virtues; 'divine powers' makes the contrast with human limits clear.

choices.english: God is present to nature, that it may be
choices.why: The clause is compressed; 'that it may be' preserves the purpose force of ut sit and the ontological point that nature exists only by God's presence.
rejected: God is present to nature, so that it exists

choices.english: nature is not absent from miracles
choices.why: Augustine's point is that even miracles involve nature as their material; 'is not absent from' keeps the negative phrasing and the paradox.

bible_refs.note: in uinum aqua, cum uoluit dominus, repente conuersa est

pass_b_english: This also solves the question of how martyrs show that they are involved in human affairs through the very favors granted to those who pray, if the dead do not know what the living are doing. For we have heard—not from uncertain rumors but from reliable witnesses—that the confessor Felix, whose dwelling you devoutly love, appeared not only through the effects of his favors but even to people's very sight when Nola was being attacked by barbarians. But such things are shown forth by God in a way far different from the usual order assigned to each kind of creature. For water was suddenly turned into wine when the Lord willed it, but that does not mean we should fail to recognize what water can do in its own proper order among the elements, apart from the rarity or rather the uniqueness of that divine work. Nor does the fact that Lazarus rose mean that every dead person rises whenever he wishes, or that a lifeless body is roused by a living person the way a sleeper is roused by someone awake. Human affairs have their limits; signs of divine powers are something else. Some things happen naturally, others miraculously—though God is present to nature, that it may be, and nature is not absent from miracles. So we should not think that any dead person can be involved in the affairs of the living just because martyrs are present to heal or help certain people. Rather, we should understand that martyrs are involved in the affairs of the living through divine power, precisely because the dead by their own nature cannot be involved in the affairs of the living.

last_rejected.why: "inquilinatum" means tenantship/inhabiting, not dwelling; Felix's presence as inquilinus (tenant/sojourner) at Nola is meant, not a building.
last_rejected.fix: whose sojourning there you devoutly love
last_rejected.ruling: inquilinatum = dwelling/habitation; 'dwelling you love' captures the sense adequately within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: not only through the effects of his favors but even to people's very sight
last_rejected.source_quote: non enim solis beneficiorum effectibus, uerum ipsis etiam hominum aspectibus
last_rejected.why: The Latin says martyrs appear not only through effects of favors but even to sight; English makes it Felix alone, but "confessorem" is accusative after "adparuisse"—Felix appeared, not martyrs generally.
last_rejected.fix: that Felix appeared not only through the effects of his favors but even to the very sight of people
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly says Felix appeared; 'martyrs generally' is the broader context, not the translation's claim.

last_rejected.quote: a lifeless body is roused by a living person
last_rejected.why: "exanimis" is nominative singular masculine, referring to Lazarus/the dead person, not "a lifeless body"; and "a uiuente" is by a living one, not "by a living person" as agent but as subject of intransitive.
last_rejected.fix: or that one who has lost life rises by a living one
last_rejected.ruling: 'lifeless body' for exanimis and 'by a living person' for a uiuente are within normal rendering range.

last_rejected.quote: the way a sleeper is roused by someone awake
last_rejected.why: English inverts agency: Latin has sleeper roused by wakeful one, but "exanimis... excitatur" is intransitive/passive, not "roused by" as if the living one acts on him.
last_rejected.fix: or that one lifeless rises by a living one as a sleeper rises by a wakeful one
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly renders dormiens excitatur a uigilante as 'sleeper roused by someone awake'; no inversion.

last_rejected.quote: martyrs are present to heal or help certain people
last_rejected.source_quote: quibusdam sanandis uel adiuuandis martyres adsunt
last_rejected.why: "adsunt" means they are present at/to, not "present to heal" as if purpose; datives are of persons benefited, not purpose infinitives.
last_rejected.fix: martyrs are present for certain people to be healed or helped
last_rejected.ruling: Gerundive datives sanandis/adiuuandis express purpose; 'present to heal or help' captures this correctly.

last_rejected.quote: precisely because the dead by their own nature cannot be involved in the affairs of the living
last_rejected.source_quote: quoniam defuncti per naturam propriam uiuorum rebus interesse non possunt
last_rejected.why: English loses the concessive/causal precision: "ideo potius intellegendum est... quoniam" = "this should rather be understood... because"—the divine power explanation replaces the natural impossibility, not is caused by it.
last_rejected.fix: rather, it should be understood that martyrs are involved in the living's affairs through divine power, since the dead by their own nature cannot be involved in the living's affairs
last_rejected.ruling: 'precisely because' correctly renders quoniam; the causal relationship is accurately conveyed.
